questions.prompt: What makes the pattern IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...) worth recognizing on sight?
options: It is the only way to download a file in PowerShell
It fetches remote content and executes it in the same step, without writing anything to disk for a scanner to catch
It only works on PowerShell 7 and later
It requires administrator privileges to run
questions.explanation: This is the classic fileless download-cradle pattern -- IEX evaluates the fetched content as code immediately, meaning the payload never exists as a file that static antivirus scanning could catch.

questions.prompt: Why are Set-MpPreference and Add-MpPreference tampering calls considered a particularly high-signal pattern?
options: They are legitimate, documented Defender-management cmdlets -- which is exactly what makes them effective when an attacker uses them to clear the way before staging a payload
They automatically alert Microsoft when used
questions.explanation: Because these cmdlets are legitimate and documented, they blend into normal admin activity -- but an attacker disabling real-time monitoring or excluding a path immediately before dropping a payload is one of the most direct signals available.

questions.prompt: Why can PowerShell code execute without a powershell.exe or pwsh.exe process ever appearing in a process tree?
options: This is not actually possible under any circumstances
PowerShell's automation engine is a .NET library that can be hosted directly inside a different process, without requiring the standalone executable
Only Windows Server supports this behavior
questions.explanation: Because System.Management.Automation is a .NET library, any process that embeds it directly can run full PowerShell functionality -- which is exactly why engine-level logging (Script Block Logging) catches activity that process-creation monitoring alone would miss.

questions.prompt: Why is a flag like -NoProfile considered a weak signal on its own, but part of a red flag when clustered with -WindowStyle Hidden?
options: -NoProfile is always malicious regardless of context
Legitimate unattended automation routinely uses -NoProfile, so it's the combination and context -- not any single flag -- that actually signals something abnormal
-WindowStyle Hidden cannot be used legitimately under any circumstances
These flags only appear in PowerShell 2.0
questions.explanation: This lesson's recurring theme: individual flags used routinely by legitimate automation only become meaningful red flags in combination with each other and with context like the parent process.
